name: Xor of Median (Easy Version)
description: This is the easy version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, the constraints on $$$t$$$, $$$k$$$, and $$$m$$$ are lower. You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. A sequence $$$a$$$ of $$$n$$$ integers is called good if the following condition holds: Let $$$\text{cnt}_x$$$ be the number of occurrences of $$$x$$$ in sequence $$$a$$$. For all pairs $$$0 \le i \lt j \lt m$$$, at least one of the following has to be true: $$$\text{cnt}_i = 0$$$, $$$\text{cnt}_j = 0$$$, or $$$\text{cnt}_i \le \text{cnt}_j$$$. In other words, if both $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ are present in sequence $$$a$$$, then the number of occurrences of $$$i$$$ in $$$a$$$ is less than or equal to the number of occurrences of $$$j$$$ in $$$a$$$. You are given integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$. Calculate the value of the bitwise XOR of the median$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ of all good sequences $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$ with $$$0\le a_i \lt m$$$. Note that the value of $$$n$$$ can be very large, so you are given its binary representation instead. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$The median of a sequence $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$ is defined as the $$$\left\lfloor\frac{n + 1}{2}\right\rfloor$$$-th smallest value in the sequence.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 50$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$k$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le 200$$$, $$$1 \le m \le 500$$$) — the number of bits in $$$n$$$ and the upper bound on the elements in sequence $$$a$$$. The second line of each test case contains a binary string of length $$$k$$$ — the binary representation of $$$n$$$ with no leading zeros. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$k$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$200$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output a single integer representing the bitwise XOR of the median of all good sequences $$$a$$$ of length $$$n$$$ where $$$0\le a_i \lt m$$$.
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2056F1 — Xor of Median (Easy Version) [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
